source.title: Layer-Wise Feedback Alignment is Conserved in Deep Neural Networks

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Figure 4 is referenced, but its plotted values are not included in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps network width and reports test loss as a function of width, which is relevant to model-size generalization, but it does not report the test-error measure specified in V1.
record.gate_note: Figure 4 reports test-loss curves across widths for the noisy-MNIST experiments. The text does not give curve values or describe their shape. Reported CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet accuracy comparisons concern class-count difficulty and feedback-alignment methods, not the claim versions. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a study of feedback-alignment learning rules. It never mentions double descent, an interpolation threshold, or a peak in test error. Its one width sweep (noisy MNIST, widths 15–200) is presented only as evidence of benign overfitting. Figure 4's caption says all methods generalize despite fitting the noise. No result bears on any claim version. Given 784 inputs and 4k training samples, even width 15 has about 11.8k first-layer weights. So the sweep probably lies entirely past the parameter-count interpolation point and could not show a peak near it.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that a conservation law gives FA an implicit regularization toward forward–feedback alignment. They also give convergence conditions via alignment dominance, and find that better alignment (adaFA, sign-FA) improves multi-class performance. The noisy-MNIST width result is framed as benign overfitting, not as double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The study concerns feedback-alignment learning dynamics and does not apply the original double-descent method.

fits_no_version.finding: On a 4k noisy-MNIST subset with 20% label noise, two-layer leaky ReLU networks of width 15–200 fit the noise yet generalize on a clean test set. This holds under FA, adaFA, signFA and GD (Figure 4; values not in the text).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign overfitting: overparameterized two-layer networks trained with feedback alignment or gradient descent interpolate noisy labels without test loss worsening as width grows.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: For the width-dependent test-loss result, values and curve shape are available only in a referenced figure and are not present in the supplied text. The width experiment uses a noisy-MNIST subset and does not report test-error results.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep across the interpolation threshold and no test-error peak is examined. The sweep likely starts past interpolation.
Test error over epochs is not reported. Only alignment over epochs is shown.
Only neural networks are used, and no capacity curve through the interpolation point is shown.
Label noise is fixed at 20%. Regularization and multiple peaks are not studied.
No alternative parameter count is studied.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' relation was wrong. The study does not engage double descent, and its width range likely never crosses the interpolation threshold. Relation is set to 'discusses' only because no enum value fits a study that neither cites nor uses the claim; T6 is the operative classification. The CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet tables vary class count and learning rule, not capacity, and are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: The width sweep reports test loss rather than test error; no test-error values or explicit test-error curve shape are reported.
The study discusses alignment over epochs, but does not report test error over epochs.
Training sample size is not varied to test whether more data raises test error near an interpolation threshold.
The study does not test a general double-descent curve across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
The study uses 20% label noise in one experiment, but does not test how noise or regularization affects a peak, multiple descent, or its disappearance.
The study does not compare complexity measures or test whether an effective-parameter count turns a second descent into a U-shaped curve.
